title: the sounds
hook: the alphabet walks from the throat to the lips
tomorrow: how can one puff of breath turn a hand into something harsh?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Devanagari on skin: two views, both sure the letters are more than decoration. Now the letters turn into the sounds.

Open wide and say ahh, the way a doctor asks. That sound comes from far back, from the throat. Now say ka, then ga: same place, the back of the tongue against the back of the mouth. Here's the surprise. The Sanskrit consonants begin right there, at the throat, and march forward, row by row, until they end at the lips. The order isn't a list to memorize. It's a map of the mouth.
screen: `SAY AHH.` → `KA, GA: THE THROAT.` → `A MAP OF THE MOUTH.`

segments.voice: The old science of sound is called shiksha, and the Taittiriya Upanishad names it near its start, listing what it studies: the sound, its pitch, its length, its effort, and how sounds join. Panini's grammar sorts sounds by exactly that: two sounds belong together when their place in the mouth and their effort are alike. So the consonants come in rows. The throat: ka, kha, ga, gha. The palate, the middle of the tongue against the roof: cha, ja. Then the tongue curled back toward the top of the roof, for a hard ta, da and na that English doesn't quite have. Then the teeth: a soft ta and da, the tongue's tip pressed against them. Then the lips: pa, ba, ma. Throat, palate, roof, teeth, lips. Back to front. And it matters in a real line. The Gita's karmani has that curled-back n: tongue up and back, not tapping the teeth. Say it with an English n and a listener who knows the sound will hear the difference at once. A reader who knows the map can sound out a letter never seen before, just by its row.
screen: `SHIKSHA: THE SCIENCE OF SOUND.` · `SORTED BY PLACE IN THE MOUTH.` · `THROAT, PALATE, ROOF, TEETH, LIPS.` · `KARMANI'S CURLED-BACK N.`

segments.voice: Slowly, one on each out-breath, say ka, then cha, then a ta with the tongue curled back, then a ta with the tongue on the teeth, then pa, and feel the place each one is made travel forward, from throat to lips. Then walk it back the other way. If you can't speak aloud where you are, shape them silently and feel the tongue move.
The sounds: Sanskrit's consonants laid out as a map of the mouth, from the throat to the lips.
Keep this: the sounds, an alphabet that walks from the throat to the lips, one row at a time. Back tomorrow.

howItsDone: Sanskrit learners usually recite the consonants row by row, ka kha ga gha, cha chha ja jha and so on, paying attention to where each is made in the mouth, often repeating after a teacher.

fork.setup: a letter you've never seen sits in the same row as ka, kha, ga and gha. where in your mouth do you try it first?
options: at the throat: the row tells you where the sound lives.
at the lips: every sound ends up there.
anywhere: the rows are just tradition.
fork.reveal: the consonants sit in rows by place: throat, palate, roof, teeth, lips. know the row and you know the place.

notes: Answers 1438's question. First day of 'the sounds'. Taittiriya 1.2 lists varṇa, svara, mātrā, bala, sāma, santāna; the voice paraphrases five of them ('the sound, its pitch, its length, its effort, and how sounds join') and leaves sāma unnamed. Confirm.
Ashtadhyayi 1.1.9 tulyāsyaprayatnaṃ savarṇam, paraphrased. The five consonant rows (velar, palatal, retroflex, dental, labial) are standard; the voice names them in plain English.
Karmaṇi's ṇ is retroflex (ण). Day 1447 (another writer) covers vowel length; this day stays on place of articulation. Senses shape: the practice is physical (feeling the place move).
